#7887. 2026 Heating Oil Prices: Are They the Worst They’ve Ever Been, and Is There Any Way to Keep Costs From Skyrocketing?

Published Nov 2, 2026 2:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you are one of the 4 million households in the United States that rely on heating oil to power furnaces, boilers, and water heaters, you might be experiencing sticker shock when it comes to heating oil prices this season. The price has risen to about $6 per gallon compared to last year’s $3 per gallon.

According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, the cost to heat a home using heating oil is expected to rise by at least 50 percent across the region, including states like Maine, Massachusetts, and New York. In fact, Maine has been getting a lot of attention lately since the state relies heavily on this type of fuel, and prices have already reached 80 percent higher than just a year ago. Learn why heating oil is so expensive this year and what you can do to manage the “pain at the tank.”

Heating oil prices typically rise during the winter as demand increases heading into the heating season, says Lowell Richard, director of fuel operations at Townsend, a home service company based in New England that offers fuel delivery as well as HVAC and electrical services. “Over the past several months, global events and geopolitical uncertainty have driven significant increases in the cost of heating oil, propane, gasoline, diesel fuel, and other forms of energy,” he explains. With a shift in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war with Iran, the cost of heating oil has gone up. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has also impacted the global supply, leading to price hikes.

By comparison, propane prices are relatively unchanged from last year because propane has a different supply structure than heating oil. “Propane is a byproduct of both crude oil and natural gas processing, so its price is linked to both—natural gas prices tend to be steadier, while crude oil does fluctuate,” says Richard. “Additionally, propane has lower wholesale prices and adequate inventories. As a result, propane prices are typically steadier than heating oil prices.” It’s worth noting that propane prices vary by supplier and delivery volume, so Richard recommends checking with your local supplier for the current price.

If you are struggling to pay your heating bills, consider tapping into available resources in your area. “Every supplier is unique, but at Townsend, we offer several ways to help our customers spread out or control their costs,” explains Richard. “We have a variety of budget plans to help fit our customers’ financial needs. For example, automatic delivery is something we encourage because it typically offers better pricing and helps homeowners avoid emergency delivery fees.”

Fortunately, there are several ways for you to help offset high heating oil prices on your monthly bill. Try making one or more of the following changes in your home to keep heating costs manageable, and if suspect damage to your oil tank, have the tank checked and replaced if necessary.

Set your thermostat to a comfortable temperature, but keep in mind that setting it even a few degrees lower can save a noticeable amount on your energy costs, says Richard. “Intentionally setting your thermostat 7 to 10 degrees lower when you are sleeping or away can save up to 10 percent on annual heating costs,” Richard explains. Investing in a programmable or smart thermostat will help you set temperature preferences and schedules, even when you are not home.

Check all the doors, windows, and exterior walls for drafts, since your home can lose heat if ‌air is leaking out. “Replace old or missing weatherstripping around doors, windows, and pipe entry points, and seal cracks in your foundation if you have any,” suggests Richard.

Use a space heater so you can lower your thermostat a few degrees. Choose an energy-efficient model that has a thermostat, adjustable heat settings, sleep mode, and auto-off timers to avoid wasting energy. Always turn a space heater off when you leave the room.

Featuring three heating modes, quiet operation, and an attractive look, this efficient space heater earned “best overall” in our hands-on testing.

“Change your air filter every 30 to 90 days,” says Richard. “A clogged air filter will significantly impact how efficient your system is, so make this a regular habit.”

Maintain your heating system to ensure it is running as efficiently as possible, which in turn requires less energy to heat your home. “Get a fall tune-up to catch small problems before they become bigger, and therefore pricier, problems,” says Richard.

“If your water heater runs on heating oil, keep it set to 120 degrees Fahrenheit for safety and to save on energy costs,” notes Richard.

#7886. What’s Downshifting? The Trend That’s Helping Homeowners Do More With Less

Downshifting can mean a smaller home, fewer belongings, or a lighter schedule. Here's how the lifestyle works and where to start.

Sometimes less IS more. At least, that’s what one home and lifestyle trend would have you believe.

A house can demand more time and money than homeowners expect. Spare bedrooms fill up with things nobody uses, the yard needs another afternoon of work, and there’s always something that needs fixing. Downshifting is one way homeowners are trying to change that.

Here’s what downshifting means, how it’s different from downsizing, and whether it can actually save money.

A post shared by RetroSuburbia (@retrosuburbiaofficial)

Downshifting is pretty much what it sounds like. It’s a decision to slow things down a bit, spend less, and get rid of some of the things that take up too much time or space around the house.

Permaculture writer David Holmgren covers the idea in his book RetroSuburbia, which describes downshifting as “a conscious choice and action to shift to a lifestyle with less consumption, complexity, stress and status seeking.” The idea is to make everyday life a little easier to manage, whether that’s by cutting expenses or having fewer responsibilities.

It sounds a lot like downsizing, but the two aren’t quite the same. Downsizing usually means moving to a smaller house or getting rid of belongings. Downshifting doesn’t necessarily involve moving at all.

One family might trade a large house for a smaller place that needs less maintenance. Another might stay right where they are, stop buying things they don’t need, or spend less time working on the house.

Homeowners can start by looking at what’s taking up the most time or money. Maybe that’s a garage full of things that haven’t been used in years, or a spare bedroom that’s become a storage room. Clearing out those spaces can mean less to clean and look after.

Other changes can be pretty small, too. Borrowing a tool instead of buying one, fixing furniture rather than replacing it, or starting a small vegetable garden are all examples. The Environmental Protection Agency also recommends buying less and reusing things to help reduce waste.

Even looking for ways to lower utility bills, like sealing drafty windows or keeping up with heating and cooling maintenance, can be part of downshifting.

One reason people consider downshifting is to save money. Buying fewer things and using less energy can certainly help, but moving to a smaller home doesn’t automatically mean smaller bills.

“New homeowners are often surprised by the costs of owning property,” according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The agency recommends putting together a budget that includes property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other expenses beyond the mortgage.

There are some practical things to consider, too. A smaller house might not have enough room for a growing family, and moving farther away could mean a longer commute. Even growing vegetables or repairing things around the house takes time.

Still, for some households, having fewer things to pay for and maintain can leave more time for family, hobbies, or just enjoying the house they already have.

And that’s really the point of downshifting. It doesn’t have to mean selling a house or getting rid of everything. Sometimes it’s as simple as deciding the house doesn’t need another project or another piece of furniture.

#7885. Does Every Home Need a Bathtub? The Pros and Cons of Going Tub-Free

Updated Nov 2, 2026 2:35 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

There are shower people, and then there are bath people. While these two groups may be able to debate the advantages and disadvantages of having a bathtub in a home from sunrise to sunset, not every home needs a bathtub and some can’t do without.

Even though a bathtub may simply be nice to have, there may be other reasons to include or exclude a bathtub if you are thinking about future resale value and your investment. With luxury showers growing in popularity, homeowners’ needs for tubs are changing.

https://secure.money.com/embeds/embedder.js?v=1

Rachel Moussa, founder and Realtor at Blushwood Realty Group in Texas, says that when she first got into he unwritten rule was that there should be one bathtub on each floor that has a bedroom. For two-level homes with bedrooms upstairs and downstairs, there should at least one tub on each floor. We get that. If you love a good tub soak, you don’t want to have to schlep your bath salts, book, beverage, candle, and other gear to another floor.

This tub-per-floor rule, Moussa says, is no longer hard and fast. Whether you’re remodeling a bathroom or contemplating a home without a bathtub, here’s what to consider if you’re thinking about ditching the tub.

From a time and water waste perspective, showers have the upper hand. The average shower in the U.S. lasts approximately 8 minutes and uses approximately 16 gallons of water. A bath is a more languid affair. Sometimes soaks can last more than a half an hour and use around 70 gallons of water, which doesn’t include the water you might use to rinse off after a bath. The less water you use bathing, the more money you can save on your water bill.

The Keenray bucket towel warmer heats up in just 6 minutes and holds up to 2 bath towels measuring 70 x 40 inches. See our full review.

Shower people may not want a bathtub of any kind in their home, and might go as far as to remove a tub from their primary suite and put in a walk-in shower. If you plan to stay in the home long-term, nixing a tub really isn’t much to worry about. However, if you plan to put your house on the market in the near future and your floor plan doesn’t include a tub, understand that you’re automatically excluding some percentage of potential buyers.

After hundreds of sales and experience in renovating and flipping houses, Moussa says there are people who will not buy a house without a bathtub. In contrast, having a bathtub in a home is highly unlikely to tank a real estate transaction. So erring on the side of at least one tub in the house could make a difference in your ability to sell your home.

Moussa points out that jetted tubs can be pretty gross if they’re not taken care of properly. The interior pipes of jetted tubs that are not filtered or cleaned with appropriate chemicals can develop bacteria and microbial growth. When the jets turn on, this bacteria shoots into the tub along with the water, which can result in adverse health effects, including urinary tract infections and skin irritations or infections.

Families with young children or pets tend to rely heavily on tubs; many would consider a quality bathtub essential. Washing little ones in the kitchen sink may work while they are really small, but there comes a point when that doesn’t work anymore; tub baths, unlike showers, can get the kids clean while you stay dry. Similarly, a bathtub is often the easiest place to scrub dogs and other pets clean after they play outdoors.

RELATED: The Best Tub-to-Shower Conversion Kits to Update the Bathroom

Walk-in showers are generally better than tubs for seniors or those with mobility issues. Showers are easier to get into and out of than tubs are, and are thus usually preferred by those who are aging in place.

However, as Moussa mentions, houses do shift a little over time, so a curbless shower built at the right angle now may create an opportunity for water to pool years down the road. A shower that has even a small lip or curb can contain water better and eliminate future stress. Accessible walk-in tubs, which have with a side door to the bathtub for easy entry, are another option.

How often you plan to have a long, luxurious bath is another factor. If you don’t have a hot tub at your home, a hot bath is the next best thing. Creating a spa-like environment is a benefit many homeowners seek out when looking for a primary suite with a bathroom. A bathtub with a ledge around the top or near a source of natural light is another benefit that adds to the ambiance.

Many adults like baths because of the luxury associated with them, but Moussa points out that modern showers can be extravagant too. Large showers with frameless glass elevate the aesthetic of a bathroom. These showers often have multiple shower heads and settings, built-in seating, and plenty of space to shower without feeling cramped. The steam keeps you warm, and you get a constant water supply at your preferred temperature, unlike a tub where the water gets gradually cooler.

#7884. Chemerinsky: Supreme Court once again examines conflicts over the free exercise of religion

On Tuesday, the U.S. Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in a major case about free exercise of religion, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. Over the last decade, the justices have greatly expanded First Amendment protections for religion. This case could either go much further in that direction or show a court that is willing to allow the government to stop discrimination even when it infringes on religious beliefs.

The case involves a Colorado law launched in 2023 that provides for universal preschool education. Under the program, the state will pay for preschool at any public, secular private or religious school. To receive funds, the school must agree that it will not discriminate against children based on their parents’ race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, income or lack of housing.

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, and another Catholic preschool in the Archdiocese of Denver declined to sign the agreement, saying that it conflicts with church teachings on marriage, sex and gender. Their objection is to having to agree to take children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender. They argue that excluding the religious schools from the universal program denies them a public benefit due to their religious beliefs.

The federal district court and the Denver-based 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected their challenge and upheld the Colorado law. Both courts relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Employment Division v. Smith (1990), which held that the free exercise clause of the First Amendment cannot be used to require exceptions from general laws. That case involved Native Americans who sought an exemption from an Oregon law prohibiting the consumption of peyote on the grounds that its use was a part of their religious rituals. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote the opinion for the court ruling against the Native Americans. The court said that so long as the law was neutral, not motivated by a desire to infringe religion, and so long as it applied to everyone, it could not be challenged as denying free exercise of religion.

The federal district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law prohibiting discrimination by preschools, concluding that it was a neutral law of general applicability. These courts also held that there was no discrimination against religious schools in their ability to receive public funds. In a series of cases—Trinity Lutheran v. Comer (2017), Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020), and Carson v. Makin (2022)—the court held that it violates free exercise of religion for the government to deny funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools. The Colorado law was upheld because it does not discriminate against religious schools; it provides funds to faith-based preschools on the same terms as all other preschools.

The plaintiffs sought certiorari, and the Supreme Court granted review on two questions. (1) Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Employment Division v. Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct; (2) whether Carson v. Makin displaces the rule of Employment Division v. Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.

The last major Supreme Court decision concerning the application of Employment Division v. Smith was Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021). The city of Philadelphia contracts with private social service agencies to help place children in foster homes. Every contract is explicit in prohibiting the agency from discriminating on the basis of race, sex, religion and sexual orientation.

Catholic Social Services long had participated in this aspect of the program but in recent years has declined to do so because of the contractual requirement that it not discriminate based on sexual orientation. CSS says that its religious beliefs prevent it from providing inspections or placing children with same sex-couples.

The agency challenged the nondiscrimination requirement as violating its First Amendment rights. The district court and the Philadelphia-based 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected these arguments. Both courts relied on Employment Division v. Smith.

The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the lower courts and ruled in favor of Catholic Social Services. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion for the court. He said that under Employment Division v. Smith a “law is not generally applicable if it ‘invite[s]’ the government to consider the particular reasons for a person’s conduct by providing a ‘mechanism for individualized exemptions.’” The Philadelphia ordinance gave city officials the authority to grant exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement. The court said that it was irrelevant that none ever had been granted and that there was no evidence of discrimination against religious entities. The existence of discretion was enough for it to not be a neutral law of general applicability. Therefore, it had to meet strict scrutiny. The court concluded that the city failed to meet strict scrutiny and that its policy was therefore unconstitutional.

Justice Samuel Alito concurred in the judgment and was joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch. In a 77-page opinion, Justice Alito expressly called for the court to overrule Smith. Justice Alito argued at length against the Smith approach and stated: “We should reconsider Smith without further delay. The correct interpretation of the free exercise clause is a question of great importance, and Smith’s interpretation is hard to defend. It can’t be squared with the ordinary meaning of the text of the free exercise clause or with the prevalent understanding of the scope of the free-exercise right at the time of the First Amendment’s adoption.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote a concurring opinion that was joined in full by Justice Brett Kavanaugh. She expressed agreement with many of the criticisms of Smith advanced by Justice Alito. But she said that there are hard questions as to what test should replace the one from Smith. She said that the court did not need to address that in this case because the city of Philadelphia policy was unconstitutional “regardless whether Smith stays or goes.”

The Supreme Court did not grant certiorari in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on the question of whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith, but that issue very much underlies the issues before the court.

Petitioner St. Mary’s Catholic Parish clearly is urging the court to jettison Smith. The first argument in its brief is that the “court rarely applies Smith.” It says: “Out of the 18 free exercise cases this court has resolved since Smith in 1990, this court has relied on Smith only twice to rule against the religious objector,” and one of these was Smith itself.

There also is the underlying question of whether a religious belief should be a basis for an exemption from antidiscrimination laws. In Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises Inc. (1968), the court summarily rejected a claim that a person’s religious beliefs were a basis for their discriminating in violation of civil rights statutes. If the court overrules Smith, or says that strict scrutiny should be used under Smith, the question will need to be addressed: Should free exercise of religion provide a right to harm others by discriminating against them?

For decades, the Supreme Court decided cases about when government aid to religious schools violated the establishment clause of the First Amendment. But over the last decade, the court has held that the denial of funding to religious schools when it is provided to private secular schools violates the free exercise clause of the First Amendment. For example, in its most recent ruling, Carson v. Makin (2022), the court held that it violated free exercise of religion for the state to pay for secular private schools but not religious schools for children in rural areas where there are not public schools.

The district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law on the ground that it provided aid to all preschools—public, secular private, and faith-based—on exactly the same terms. But St. Mary’s Catholic Parish argues that Colorado is denying it funding because of its exercising its religious beliefs and excluding children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender.

In the prior cases about funding, the state laws expressly excluded religious schools. The Colorado law does not do that. Is it enough for a free exercise violation that its effect is to deny funding to schools that have a religious basis for their discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity?

In recent years, the conservative majority on the Supreme Court has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause of the First Amendment while simultaneously significantly increasing the safeguards under the free exercise clause. It has shown support for those who want to violate anti-discrimination laws on account of their religious beliefs. St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy will be important in indicating whether the court will go even further in these directions.

Erwin Chemerinsky is dean of the University of California at Berkeley School of Law. He is an expert in constitutional law. He’s also the author of many books, including his most recent ones: Campus Speech and Academic Freedom: A Guide for Difficult Times and The Supreme Court October Term 2024: Taking Sides.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7883. Fifth Circuit Will Decide En Banc Whether § 230 Preempts Texas Mandates on Social Media Platforms

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Fifth Circuit ordered en banc rehearing Wednesday; here's an excerpt from the long panel opinion (Computer & Comm. Industry Ass'n v. Paxton), decided in July by Fifth Circuit Judges Dana Douglas and Patrick Higginbotham (I posted about the case then):

[1.] [Texas] H.B. 18 … imposes requirements on DSPs [Digital Service Providers]…. With the exception of its age-verification requirement, H.B. 18 applies only to DSPs whose digital service "connects users in a manner that allows users to socially interact with other users on the digital service," "allows a user to create a public or semi-public profile for purposes of signing into and using the digital service," and "allows a user to create or post content that can be viewed by other users of the digital service," including via a message board, chat room, or other "landing page, video channel, or main feed that presents to a user content created and posted by other users."

{H.B. 18 exempts from its coverage state and local government websites, financial institutions, medical websites, small businesses, higher education websites, employee management software, school education software, and e-mail and direct messaging services that provide only those services. H.B. 18 also exempts digital services that "primarily function[ ] to provide a user with access to news, sports, commerce, or content primarily generated or selected by the [DSP]" and provide only incidental social functions.}

H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement mandates covered DSPs to develop and implement a strategy to prevent known minors' exposure to "harmful material" and other content "that promotes, glorifies, or facilitates" "suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders"; "substance abuse"; "stalking, bullying, or harassment"; and "grooming, trafficking, child pornography, or other sexual exploitation or abuse." "Harmful material" is defined with reference to its definition in the Texas Penal Code [to refer to obscene-as-to-minors sexually themed material]….

[2.] Consistent with other courts of appeal, we have interpreted Section 230 to provide DSPs with "broad immunity" from "all claims stemming from their publication of information created by third parties." … Building on Doe v. MySpace, Inc. (5th Cir. 2018), where we had previously held that Section 230 "shielded MySpace from negligence liability for publishing communications between a minor and an adult who later sexually assaulted her," in Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton (5th Cir. 2024), we held that an age-verification requirement for pornographic websites was different, and not preempted, because it did not pertain to "immuniz[ing] web service providers from harm caused by unremoved speech on their website," which is "the point of Section 230."

We distinguished between liability "reliant on the harm done by third-party content," which is preempted by Section 230, and "liability purely based on whether plaintiffs comply with the statute," which is not. "[T]he nature of Section 230's protections," we observed, is "to protect a provider from speaker-liability stemming from the speech it hosts." …

[T]he monitoring and filtering requirement requires covered DSPs to "implement a strategy" to prevent known minors' exposure to "harmful material"—that is, material obscene to minors as it is defined by Texas law—and other content "that promotes, glorifies, or facilitates" "suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders"; "substance abuse"; "stalking, bullying, or harassment"; and "grooming, trafficking, child pornography, or other sexual exploitation or abuse." It provides for enforcement for "violation[s]" by the Consumer Protection Division of the Attorney General's Office or by actions for a declaratory judgment or an injunction brought by the parent of a "known minor affected by" a violation.

Actions to enforce the monitoring and filtering requirement are claims stemming from DSPs' actions as publishers, that is, from their monitoring, screening, and deletion of content, and are thus squarely preempted by Section 230. Although H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement is framed as a matter of affirmative obligations rather than direct penalties for published content, this is not conclusive under our precedent.

"[I]f the claim seeks to hold the defendant liable for 'deciding whether to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content[,]' the claim treats the defendant as a publisher or speaker and is barred by section 230." The requirement would hold DSPs liable for their failure to adhere to state-set publication standards, not only "treat[ing] [them] as … publisher[s] or speaker[s]," but treating them as publishers subject to sweeping state controls. Enforcement is triggered by failures to adequately filter according to a complex array of prescribed practices, as ascertained by the Texas Attorney General's Office and by the parents of minors "affected"—in other words, harmed—by these failures. The monitoring and filtering requirement thus imposes a "duty" that "'would necessarily require an internet company to monitor[, alter, or remove] third-party content.'"

As we observed in Free Speech Coalition, "publishers do not filter audiences; they filter content." Unlike the age-verification requirement we addressed in that case, H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement is all about filtering content, and is thus preempted….

[3.] The Attorney General contends that the Supreme Court's recent recognition of the DSPs' own free speech interest in curating the content they display in Moody v. NetChoice, LLC (2024) means that Section 230's broadly-interpreted rule against "treat[ing]" the DSPs "as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider" does not apply to claims that simply seek to hold social media platforms liable for their own speech, such as the methods they use to curate content.

We hesitate to read Moody to render Section 230 so easily avoidable, as if speech could not be both protected by the First Amendment and subject to preemption on the grounds that the speaker may not be treated as a publisher. Such a narrow view of Section 230 preemption would conflict with the statute's purpose "to maintain the robust nature of Internet communication and, accordingly, to keep government interference in the medium to a minimum." It would also conflict with the text of § 230(c)(1), which, in spite of its often-discussed connection with specific instigating judicial decisions, "cannot be ignored": "Congress grabbed a bazooka to swat [a] fly."

Given that "First Amendment values … drive the CDA," it should be no surprise if the two protections overlap. As we recognized in MySpace, drawing on the Fourth Circuit's influential Zeran decision, "[digital] service providers … subject to liability only for the publication of information, and not for its removal … would have a natural incentive simply to remove messages upon notification [of a possible harm,] whether the contents were [actually harmful] or not." This would have an obvious "chilling effect on the freedom of Internet speech," implicating basic First Amendment freedoms as well as Section 230's more specific protections for internet speech.

Viewing our Section 230 precedent together with Moody, the First Amendment protects the DSPs' editorial discretion from unconstitutional government regulation, and Section 230 protects those same decisions from civil liability based on third-party content. The argument that we must choose between them presents a false choice….

Because we hold that the monitoring and filtering requirement is preempted by Section 230 of the CDA, we do not reach the constitutional issues presented here.

Judge James Ho dissented as to that analysis:

[1.] Section 230 is triggered only when a provider is treated as the "publisher" or "speaker" of content provided by "another" information content provider. So it does not apply when a provider is held liable for its own content—including its curation of third-party content….

[C]uration of third-party content is fundamentally different from publication of third-party content. A digital service provider may choose to publish content created by third parties. But the providers engage in their own speech when they curate that content. The Supreme Court has so held. See Moody v. NetChoice (2024)….

[To quote Doe ex rel. Roe v. Snap, Inc. (2024) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari),] when "platforms organize users' content into newsfeeds or other compilations," they claim that they are "engage[d] in constitutionally protected speech." Yet "[w]hen it comes time for platforms to be held accountable for their websites, however, they argue the opposite." "In the platforms' world, they are fully responsible for their websites when it results in constitutional protections, but the moment that responsibility could lead to liability, they can disclaim any obligations and enjoy greater protections from suit than nearly any other industry." …

Consistent with Justice Thomas's observations, … we concluded that "section 230 does not provide a general immunity against all claims derived from third-party content." To the contrary, "providers of interactive computer services may be held liable for speech or conduct that is properly attributable to them, even if third-party speech exists somewhere upstream." …

[2.] The Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment Act (SCOPE Act) … protects children from the dangers of social media. It does so by requiring digital service providers to implement [reasonable steps] to prevent children from being exposed to "harmful material"—namely, content that promotes suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, substance abuse, stalking, bullying, harassment, grooming, trafficking, child pornography, and other sexual exploitation or abuse…. And if a platform fails to take such steps, parents may seek declaratory or injunctive relief against the provider….

[T]he Act simply imposes a duty on social media companies to meet certain standards for curation—that is, for their own speech. It imposes no penalty based on the publication of third-party speech.

So if third-party content leads to harm to children, the SCOPE Act does not hold social media companies liable, so long as they have met its standards for curation…. [T]he SCOPE Act considers the curation decisions made by social media companies—not the harm caused by the third-party content itself….

[3.] As for the First Amendment challenge to the SCOPE Act not reached by the panel majority: "States have a profound interest in protecting the innocence of children," and "[n]othing in the First Amendment prevents states from taking steps to shield children" from harmful content. I would have simply certified the questions regarding the proper interpretation of the SCOPE Act to allow the Supreme Court of Texas to clarify the meaning of state law….

Thanks to the Media Law Resource Center (MLRC) MediaLawDaily for the pointer.

#7881. Airbnb Just Did Something Guests Have Been Asking for Years — Here’s What Changed

Airbnb is putting limits on checkout chores, including washing dishes and stripping beds. Here's what hosts can still ask guests to do.

Everyone loves a vacation. But the cleanup and tidying as the trip is finishing up? Not so much.

It’s not always clear what guests are responsible for cleaning. Dishes, sheets, towels, and taking out the trash are sometimes part of checkout instructions at Airbnb rentals. With checkout typically at 11 a.m., the last morning of a trip can turn into a mad dash through an unreasonably long chore list, even when a cleaning fee has been tacked onto the bill.

That frustration, along with a growing number of travelers returning to hotels for more consistent quality and fees, is behind Airbnb’s new checkout rules. Learn which tasks guests may still face, and how hosts are responding.

Starting with reservations booked on or after November 20, 2026, Airbnb will require hosts to clearly explain their house rules and checkout requests before guests book. Hosts won’t be allowed to add new requirements through messages or signs inside the rental after a reservation is confirmed.

“House Rules are now displayed more prominently on your listing, where guests can easily see them before they book,” according to Airbnb’s announcement. Guests can also find these instructions in their Trips tab and reservation reminders.

Under the new policy, hosts generally can’t require guests to strip beds, start laundry, wash and put away dishes, or take trash to an off-site disposal facility. However, hosts can still request simpler tasks, such as placing dirty dishes in the sink, gathering used towels, or putting trash and recycling in designated bins. Guests may also be asked to turn off lights and return keys before leaving.

Airbnb’s policy distinguishes between house rules and requests. “Guests must follow hosts’ house rules, and are encouraged to comply with hosts’ requests,” according to the company. Some exceptions may apply. For example, rentals in areas with bears may require guests to use animal-proof trash containers, while drought restrictions could affect water use.

Guests are still responsible for leaving the property reasonably tidy. Airbnb’s ground rules for guests prohibit excessive messes and require guests to take responsibility for damage beyond normal wear and tear. Hosts can still charge standard cleaning fees and request reimbursement for unexpected cleaning costs or damage.

Hosts who don’t follow Airbnb’s new checkout rules could receive warnings or requests to update their listings. Repeated violations may lead to notices on their listings or lower placement in search results. Hosts can also appeal flagged requests.

The policy also prevents hosts from charging their own fines for missed chores or restricting access to amenities already included in a reservation.

However, not every host supports the changes. Some believe washing dishes after cooking is a reasonable responsibility for guests, while others worry the new rules could increase cleaning costs. A Change.org petition has called on Airbnb to reverse its restrictions on requiring guests to wash dishes.

Guests who encounter unexpected chores or requests that violate the new policy can contact Airbnb for help.

There are a few things that matter when it comes to testing the best infrared heaters. For one, they must be safe, so they need a sturdy build and/or safety features. Next, they need to produce the right amount of heat.

To test them, we set up each of the heaters according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Some could sit on the floor, while others needed to hang from the wall or the ceiling. We set them up, turned them on, and checked features like remote controls and timers.

First, we examined each radiant heater to see how sturdy or secure it appeared to be. If a heater could tip over, we made sure the safety shutoff worked. We also cranked the heaters as high as they could go to check the surfaces around the mounted heaters for safe temperatures.

Next, we checked the output. We turned each electric infrared heater up to the max setting to see how quickly they’d heat up, and we played with the thermostats to ensure they were working properly. From there, we compared the design and build quality between each model.

Infrared rays are uniquely capable of cutting through empty space and bringing warmth to the objects they strike; in fact, that’s how the sun heats the earth. Today’s infrared heaters bring warmth to objects, like clothes and skin rather than the surrounding air—an efficient mechanism in stark contrast to convection heaters, which warm the surrounding air before heating objects in that space.

Although heating the air may distribute heat more uniformly throughout a room, much energy is wasted heating unoccupied space, such as high ceilings or the outdoor air. Infrared heaters use 100 percent of the heat they produce to bring focused warmth to the objects in the path of its rays, making them much more energy efficient. An infrared heater’s energy efficiency, space coverage, and other features will vary depending on certain factors. Shoppers may want to keep the following considerations in mind while on the hunt for the best infrared heater for their homes.

When determining the right size of an infrared heater to buy, think about the square footage of the space you want to warm. Generally, infrared heaters are relatively small and portable. More powerful units for bigger areas are available, but they’re typically larger. Also, consider how much floor space an infrared heater will take up; this will vary depending on whether the unit sits vertically (in the case of a tower heater) or horizontally (like most standard heaters).

The size of the space you want to warm will also influence how powerful your heater should be. The amount of heat generated by these devices, measured in BTUs, influences the size of the space they can heat.

The BTU output of an infrared heater generally correlates with the number of watts the heater uses, which can range between 300 and 1,500 watts. (Most are capped at 1,500 watts because that’s the maximum amount a standard 110V household electrical outlet can handle.) With convection space heaters, 1 watt is equivalent to 3.412 BTUs, so it’s simple to determine the size of a space they can warm; it’s not so easy with infrared heaters.

Infrared heaters can use various heating elements, such as quartz (the most common and most efficient), ceramic, and carbon, to produce and emit infrared rays with varying levels of energy efficiency. Supplemental fans or blowers aren’t necessary, but they can provide both focused infrared heat and diffused heat through convection.

These factors impact how an infrared heater’s power rating will affect its heat output and space coverage. Just because an infrared heater boasts a higher power rating doesn’t mean it produces more heat and provides greater space coverage—much depends on the individual characteristics of the heater.

One way to calculate the general amount of power a heater should generate is to multiply the space’s square footage by 10. For example, a 100-square-foot room (10 feet by 10 feet) will need a 1,000-watt heater (100 x 10 = 1,000).

The location of an infrared heater warrants consideration due to its unique heating action. Whether it’s for outdoor use or a space heater for a basement, generally, it’s a good idea to place an infrared heater directly in front of what you want to warm. But, to be on the safe side, we consulted HVAC expert Bohannon to see where infrared heaters should be placed, and he recommends that “infrared heaters should not be placed near flammable materials such as curtains, furniture, or paper,” he says. He adds to always maintain adequate clearance around the heater to avoid any fire hazards. “It’s also important to follow the manufacturer’s guidelines regarding safe distances from walls and other objects,” Bohannon says.

The fact that they operate by emitting heat waves directly to objects (as opposed to the surrounding air) also makes them well suited to outdoor spaces, such as patios, since the heat won’t dissipate in the surrounding air. Similarly, infrared heaters are a good option for rooms with large ceilings since users needn’t worry about heated air rising and wasting away in the ceiling space.

An infrared heater needn’t be an eyesore, as there are various designs to complement different styles of home decor. Shoppers can find heaters with wood, plastic, and metal finishes, all in various colors.

The shape of the heater will depend on whether it sits on the floor vertically or horizontally, which affects not only its function but its visual form as well. Some infrared heaters simulate the appearance of a fireplace with visual and auditory effects like flames and crackling.

Infrared heaters can range from highly portable to completely stationary units. The majority are for supplemental space heating, so they’re usually portable. Some models are portable by design; they’re tidily compact and include carry handles and caster wheels. Handles and wheels are helpful for larger, heavier units that would otherwise be difficult to move. Other models, like those that hang from the wall and ceiling, aren’t portable at all.

Space heaters are a leading cause of house fires, so choosing an infrared heater with safety features is important. This is especially true for homes with pets or children who could knock the unit over. Fortunately, many manufacturers do incorporate several safety features, including:

Look for a heater with at least two of these safety features, but the more, the better. For added confidence, find a heater that’s certified by a third-party inspection agency, such as Underwriter Laboratory (with a UL logo), Intertek (stamped with the letters ETL and corresponding logo/emblem), or Canadian Standards Association (stamped with a CSA logo/emblem).

Some infrared heaters boast bells and whistles to increase functionality. These may include:

Energy-efficient infrared heaters are capable of heating the objects in a space more quickly than other types of heaters, such as convection-style units that must warm the surrounding air before they can heat the objects. They’re also usually quieter than other heaters since they don’t require fans—and those units that do have fans aren’t usually very loud. The warmth infrared heaters create won’t increase humidity or dry the air in the room, so the heat is more comfortable. Other benefits include:

If you still have questions about infrared heaters, see the answers to some common questions below for greater clarity.

No. In fact, they can use considerably less than other heaters because of how efficiently they heat up a space.

While infrared heaters are intrinsically safer than most other types of heaters, they should only be left on overnight if they have integrated safety features like an automatic tip-over shutoff, an overheat shutoff, and a shut-off timer.

Infrared heaters should only be used in the locations they are designed for. Consequently, only infrared wall heaters should be mounted on a wall.

Infrared heaters provide direct heat, so you’ll want to place it facing the area where you want to concentrate the warmth. Make sure there aren’t obstructions in the way.

Expect home infrared heaters to last about the same amount of time as other space heaters; a few years, with some good products (that are also well taken care of) lasting over a decade.

Yes, it’s possible to heat an entire house with infrared heating. However, it is usually done with larger infrared heating panels, not the more compact units like those on this list. The smaller heaters in this guide are best for supplementary heating, as a toasty addition to your home heating system.

#7879. How Does Google Maps Know There’s Traffic Before You Hit It?

A map app can spot a traffic jam before drivers reach it. Here’s how phones detect slowdowns, predict delays, and sometimes get it wrong.

Most drivers know this experience. They’re en route somewhere when their smartphone map app starts pushing back their ETA. Soon, brake lights appear ahead as traffic slows to a crawl.

But how did the navigation app know about the traffic before the driver encountered it? Popular navigation apps like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze use real-time location data from drivers’ phones to detect slowdowns and estimate traffic conditions.

Learn what’s happening and why the estimates aren’t always right.

Map apps combine location data from many phones to understand traffic conditions on the road. Google explains that it uses combined location data for this, and Waze says drivers share real-time information just by driving with the app open. When enough drivers slow down in the same area, the app can show a backup on the map.

Apps also use past traffic information to predict delays before drivers encounter them. “To predict what traffic will look like in the near future, Google Maps analyzes historical traffic patterns for roads over time,” Google’s wevsite states.

These predictions help apps estimate arrival times and suggest alternate routes when traffic starts building.

“Our predictive traffic models are also a key part of how Google Maps determines driving routes,” the Google website continues. “If we predict that traffic is likely to become heavy in one direction, we’ll automatically find you a lower-traffic alternative. We also look at a number of other factors, like road quality. Is the road paved or unpaved, or covered in gravel, dirt or mud?”

Drivers can also report problems such as accidents and hazards through Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze, though the options vary by app and region. These reports help explain why traffic has slowed down. Google says it also uses data from local governments, which can flag road restrictions such as construction.

The colored lines on the map show where traffic is building. In most navigational systems, green means no traffic delays, orange means medium traffic, and red means delays, with darker red indicating slower speeds.

Traffic updates are generally useful, but they aren’t always accurate. Apple, for example, says it displays incident markers only when it has a high level of confidence in the reports it receives, so a new incident may take time to appear. Coverage also varies depending on how much information the apps receive. On less-traveled roads, fewer drivers may contribute location data, making it harder for apps to detect slowdowns in real time.

Arrival times are estimates, too. Google says its predictions combine historical patterns with live conditions, but it also notes that historical patterns aren’t always reliable indicators of what the road will look like. Conditions can also change unexpectedly because of events like snowstorms.

Map apps can help drivers avoid delays, but their estimates aren’t guaranteed. Drivers still need to follow road signs and pay attention to the conditions around them.

#7878. Prof. Francesca Gino's Contract and Discrimination Claims Against Harvard Business School Dismissed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"In 2021, allegations were brought against [Gino] claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty," and eventually to her tenure being revoked and her being fired.

Some short excerpts from the long decision by Judge Myong Joun (D. Mass.) today in Gino v. President & Fellows of Harvard College:

Plaintiff Francesca Gino is a former tenured professor at Harvard Business School ("HBS") and brings this action against Defendants President and Fellows of Harvard College ("Harvard") and Defendant Srikant Datar ("Dean Datar"). In 2021, allegations were brought against Plaintiff claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty. In March 2023, the investigation committee found, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Plaintiff committed research misconduct…. In May 2025, Harvard revoked Plaintiff's tenure and terminated her appointment with HBS.

Plaintiff claims that Harvard breached its obligations under various policies and procedures governing the investigation of the research misconduct allegations and the tenure revocation proceedings. Specifically, Plaintiff argues that a jury could find that Harvard deviated from its policies and procedures such that Harvard could be found in breach of those agreements, and that Harvard did not carry its burden of proving research misconduct or grave misconduct. Plaintiff also alleges that the proceedings and related findings, including the adverse employment actions taken against her, were pretext for gender discrimination….

In approximately June of 2021, three professors—Leif Nelson, Joseph Simmons, and Uri Simonsohn, who publish under the name "Data Colada"—presented their allegations against Gino to HBS Professor Max Bazerman during a 90-minute Zoom call…. [Eventually, a Harvard] Investigation Committee issued its 41-page Final Report with nearly 1,200 pages of supporting documents, finding by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff committed research misconduct intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly with regard to all five allegations.

The Investigation Committee's Final Report considered and rejected Plaintiff's contentions that unnamed "bad actors," research assistants, or other co-authors might have instead been responsible for the data anomalies. The Investigation Committee concluded that Plaintiff's "repeated and strenuous argument for a scenario of data falsification by bad actors across four different studies," involving "different co-authors, different journals, different lab personnel, and different home institutions" and spanning eight years, was "highly implausible." The Investigation Committee recommended corrections of the scientific record, putting Plaintiff on unpaid leave, and initiation of steps leading to termination of employment….

The court granted summary judgment on all these issues, in Harvard's favor. Here's an excerpt of the discussion of her breach of contract claims:

Massachusetts courts enforce contractual promises made by private universities, while according appropriate respect to their academic and disciplinary judgments. The Third Statute [a Harvard academic policy] permits removal of an officer holding a teaching appointment "only for grave misconduct or neglect of duty." I hold that this is a substantive, enforceable limitation on removal, not a merely aspirational statement.

The limitation does not, however, confer a right to have a federal jury independently determine scientific authorship, data provenance, or the correct weight of forensic evidence after an academic tribunal has considered those matters. Judicial review asks whether Harvard reached its determination honestly and reasonably, upon a rational evidentiary foundation, and in compliance with its enforceable contractual procedures. This is meaningful review: the University's decision does not prevail merely because a committee announced it.

This standard respects both the contractual restriction on removal and the institutional responsibility to adjudicate research-integrity matters. A court may not uphold a decision procured through dishonesty, resting on no reasonable evidence, or reached through a material violation of promised procedures. It also may not choose among plausible competing forensic interpretations merely because a reasonable factfinder could have drawn different scientific inferences. Gino bears the burden of proving breach in this action. The Third Statute Procedures separately placed on Harvard's complainant a clear-and-convincing burden of establishing grave misconduct or neglect of duty; the record must be examined for whether Harvard applied that burden, not treated as though the civil burden had transferred to Harvard….

Harvard's decision had a substantial contemporaneous evidentiary basis. The record describes forensic examination of anomalous data in four research papers; analysis of the history and characteristics of relevant datasets; consideration of Gino's explanations; a faculty investigation finding misconduct by a preponderance of the evidence, and; a subsequent hearing committee finding, by clear and convincing evidence, of misconduct grave enough to warrant revocation. These are not independent judicial findings that Gino altered any data. They establish that Harvard investigated defined allegations and articulated an evidentiary explanation for its decision. The committees' findings alone would not rescue a decision shown to be knowingly false or irrational; the investigative materials, considered together with the contrary submissions, provide the relevant basis for review.

Gino denies intentionally falsifying research data, relies on favorable accounts from coauthors and colleagues, and challenges aspects of the forensic inferences and evidence of access or authorship. I credit these disputes and draw permissible inferences in her favor.

But the question under the contract is not whether a jury could reject some of Harvard's inferential steps or prefer an alternative forensic account. Gino must identify evidence from which a reasonable jury could conclude that Harvard did not honestly believe its determination or lacked a rational basis to make it.

The identified differences over inference, attribution, and scientific weight do not establish that the peer decisionmakers knowingly adopted a false conclusion or acted without a reasonable evidentiary foundation. Accordingly, no triable breach arises merely from the competing interpretations of the underlying research record….

And from the court's rejection of Gino's sex discrimination theory:

Plaintiff points to the following pieces of evidence that she argues supports evidence of discriminatory animus: (1) Harvard deviated from and breached its policies and procedures; (2) Harvard and Dean Datar have historically subjected women to less favorable treatment; (3) Harvard has treated allegations of research misconduct against male professors differently than the allegations against Plaintiff, and; (4) certain statements made by Harvard employees were false and otherwise constitute discriminatory remarks….

Plaintiff relies on similar arguments she raised in support of her breach of contract claims that Harvard deviated from its policies with respect to investigating research misconduct. "Evidence that the employer deviated from its standard procedure or policies in taking an adverse employment action against a plaintiff may be relevant to the pretext inquiry." As discussed, Plaintiff's evidence does not support a finding that Harvard breached its policies. Furthermore, Plaintiff provides no evidence that any purported deviations from Harvard's policies are connected to gender bias….

Plaintiff argues that there is evidence that Defendants have historically treated women less favorably than men. This evidence includes Plaintiff's own testimony and testimony from Plaintiff's colleague at HBS. Plaintiff provided testimony in a sworn declaration that she "personally observed that it was more difficult for women to obtain tenure at HBS than men. Indeed, about three times as many male professors get promoted as compared to female ones. In the Accounting & Management Unit, it's worse: closer to four times as many." She also stated that in 2022, she participated in an Appointment Committee meeting in which "gendered language was used to discuss the work of one female professor in the Accounting & Management Unit." When Plaintiff raised the issue to senior colleagues, one of them told Plaintiff that it "has been that way for a while." Plaintiff's declaration also states that "there had not been a single tenured woman in the Accounting & Management Unit for more than 20 years." Plaintiff's colleague, Professor Frances Frei, also testified to evidence that Dean Datar attempted to prevent another female professor from obtaining tenure.

Plaintiff's evidence is plainly insufficient. This evidence is made up of Plaintiff's own conclusory allegations that it is more difficult for women to obtain tenure, a statement made by an unknown female colleague supporting Plaintiff's belief that obtaining tenure is more difficult for women, vague allegations that unspecified "gendered language" made by unknown speakers was used when discussing an unspecified female professor, and an unsubstantiated statement from a colleague that Dean Datar attempted to "counsel out" another unspecified senior lateral hire. There are no other non-speculative facts—documents, communications, data, or otherwise—that support these conclusions or that tend to show a pattern of gender bias. Indeed, when pressed for further information about Dean Datar's alleged "pattern" of disfavoring women, Professor Frei could not provide a response.

Further, the record does not demonstrate any other evidence of a pattern or practice of discriminatory conduct or unfavorable treatment that can be applied to reasonably infer gender bias against Plaintiff….

Plaintiff points to evidence that Harvard has treated allegations of misconduct against male professors differently than allegations against Plaintiff. Plaintiff points to two examples where male professors were treated differently…. "To successfully allege disparate treatment, a plaintiff must show that others similarly situated to her in all relevant respects were treated differently by the employer." … Here …, there are important differences. For instance, in both the case of Mr. Serafeim and Mr. Soltes [the two examples pointed to by Plaintiff -EV], Harvard found that the complained-of conduct did not fall within the definition of research misconduct….

Additionally, the allegations against Mr. Serafeim had to do with a misleading footnote that was later admitted and explained to be an error, and the allegations against Mr. Soltes had to do with his conduct in connection with subjects that he interviewed. In contrast, the allegations against Plaintiff involved thirteen allegations of data falsification and fabrication in nine papers co-authored by Plaintiff, and after a preliminary assessment, five of those allegations were found to be sufficiently credible to fall within the definition of research misconduct. In short, it is Plaintiff's "burden to connect the dots" between the facts and circumstances surrounding the allegations against her and those of her male colleagues, such that a jury may find that they are similarly situated. Plaintiff has not met that burden here….

Plaintiff points to allegedly false statements made by Dean Datar and other Harvard leaders, as well as a gendered remark by a member of the Investigation Committee, as evidence of unlawful animus. Plaintiff alleges that the following false claims were made: (1) Dean Datar falsely claimed under oath that he did not make any "deal" with Data Colada and Data Colada's allegations against Gino were not brought to his attention until after the Interim Policy was created; (2) Dean Datar falsely denied telling Dean Pisano that Data Colada was pressuring HBS to move the investigation along and accusing it of "whitewashing"; (3) Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino; (4) Professor Amabile falsely claimed under oath that, during the time of the investigation, she was not aware that the allegations brought against Gino were raised by Data Colada, and; (5) RIO Bonacossa falsely claimed under oath that he was not aware of Data Colada's allegations against Gino at the time he was asked to serve as RIO and he did not tell Gino she could not obtain a forensic expert….

The facts presented by Plaintiff regarding the false statements do not prove that the adverse employment actions Harvard took against Plaintiff were motivated by gender bias or that the justification offered by Harvard was a sham. The allegedly false statements about what Dean Datar, Dean Cunningham, RIO Bonacossa, or Professor Amabile knew or when they knew it are not relevant to the reasons offered by Harvard that support their adverse employment decisions.

Additionally, the other fact disputes—whether Dean Datar made a deal with Data Colada and was pressured by Data Colada to move the investigation along, and whether Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino—are not material. The investigation that led to the adverse employment actions taken against Gino took place over nearly 18 months, involved several rounds of review by several different committees, including 26 professors, administrators, and trustees who evaluated documents, research, data, and conducted witness interviews. This investigation concluded in a 41-page report detailing the allegations, investigation process, and reasoning supporting the findings. The Third Statute Proceedings were similarly thorough and resulted in in-depth findings of fact and recommendations. Plaintiff has offered no evidence to demonstrate that Harvard's reasoning is a sham or a pretext for gender bias.

Finally, Gino points to a committee member's observation that she may have experienced professional and personal pressure after her husband lost his job. Although Gino characterizes the comment as reflecting an assumption about gender and family roles, I assume for purposes of the motion that it could carry such an implication. That does not end the inquiry: the remark must be assessed in context, including the speaker's role, whether it informed a disputed factual finding, and whether the record connects it with any adverse decision because of sex. Viewed together with Gino's other evidence, the quoted remark does not, without such a connection, establish that Harvard's stated reasons were a pretext for sex discrimination.

Considering the evidence cumulatively rather than in isolated categories, Gino identifies criticism of the procedures, comments concerning women's advancement, two male faculty members accused of different forms of impropriety, challenged statements by institutional actors, and the committee member's remark. The asserted procedural irregularities do not, without a supported causal connection, compel or permit a reasonable finding that the decisionmakers acted because of her sex. The comparator matters identified above concern materially different charges and screening decisions.

Even assuming that Gino meets the modest prima facie threshold and that some administrative statements are disputed, the total record cited does not raise a genuine dispute that Harvard's articulated research-misconduct basis was a cover for sex discrimination under federal law. Count I's selective-enforcement theory separately fails because the identified male comparators do not demonstrate selective pursuit of comparable allegations on the basis of sex. The Title VII and Title IX claims are against the institution insofar as authorized by the respective statutes; any individual liability asserted against Dean Datar must be evaluated under the applicable state-law provision rather than presumed from the federal employment claims….

Douglas E. Brayley, Jenny K. Cooper, Elena W. Davis, Stephanie D. Porges, and Laura G. Hoey (Ropes & Gray LLP) represent defendants.
